Received 14 APR 2022
Plain Language Summary The formation of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau involved the opening and
Accepted 3 OCT 2022
closing of multiple oceans (the ‘Tethyan’ oceans) and the rifting, drifting and collision of multiple continental
blocks, but quantitative paleogeographic constraints on the motions of these tectonic ‘puzzle pieces’ are scarce.
Here we present paleomagnetic data from one of the central pieces of this puzzle—the South Qiangtang
block—which allow us to determine that it was located at a latitude of ∼22°S in middle Permian time, 265
million years ago. This paleolatitude constraint further allows us to estimate the width of the Tethyan oceans on
either side of the South Qiangtang block in the middle Permian, providing a first-order snapshot of the evolving
paleogeographic puzzle that gave rise to the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau.
1. Introduction
The Qinghai-Tibet Plateau comprises a mosaic of geologically distinct Paleozoic and Mesozoic blocks, including
the Qaidam block, Songpan-Ganzi block, Qiangtang block(s), Lhasa block and Himalayan block (Figure 1a). It
is generally acknowledged that some of these blocks originated from the northern margin of Gondwana, splitting
from it in the Carboniferous or Permian before subsequently drifting northward to collide with Laurasia in the
Mesozoic (Metcalfe, 2009, 2013; Stampfli et al., 2013; Zhai et al., 2013). These blocks may have rifted from
Gondwana in concert with Iran, Afghanistan and other blocks in the west (Sengör et al., 1988) and Sibumasu
in the east (Hennig et al., 2009; Peng et al., 2013), together forming an elongate continental ribbon — the
‘Cimmerian continent’. This simple tectonic narrative associates the late Paleozoic spalling and northward drift
of the Cimmerian continent with the opening and spreading of the Neo-Tethys Ocean, and the later arrival of the
Cimmerian continent to the southern margin of Laurasia is taken to mark the closure of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean.
© 2022. American Geophysical Union.
All Rights Reserved.

### page_2

Figure 1.
However, there is a lack of basic quantitative constraints on the time-dependent size of the Neo- and Paleo-Tethys
oceans. Furthermore, it is becoming increasingly clear that the specific kinematic evolution of the Tethyan realm
was likely more complicated, and involved more than just the northward drift of a single string of continental
blocks.

### page_3
Tectonics 10.1029/2022TC007355
Of particular importance is the nature and history of the Qiangtang block(s). Simple models of Tethyan evolution
have treated the Qiangtang block as a unified block that rifted from northern Gondwana and drifted northward
in concert with the rest of the Cimmerian constituents. However, geological investigations have increasingly
suggested the Qiangtang block to be a complex of two continental blocks that were independent until early
Mesozoic time: a North Qiangtang block (NQB) and a South Qiangtang block (SQB), separated by a Triassic
suture (the Longmu Co-Shuanghu Suture Zone; LSS) (e.g., Li, 1987; Liu et al., 2019; Tang & Zhang, 2014;
Zhai et al., 2011; Zhang, Cai, et al., 2006; Zhang, Zhang, et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2016). This potential late
Paleozoic independence of the NQB and SQB has important implications for the structure and kinematic evolu-
tion of Tethyan realm more broadly, because it implies that the constituents of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau do not
represent a single ‘wave’ of continental blocks from northern Gondwana. It also challenges the concept of a
singular ‘Paleo-Tethys Ocean’, because both the LSS and the northern boundary of the NQB have been proposed
to represent ‘Paleo-Tethyan’ sutures, in addition to the Eastern Kunlun-Animaqing suture even further north
(Figure 1a). Unfortunately, we cannot yet exploit the paleogeographic history of the Qiangtang blocks to better
resolve the development of the Tethyan realm because there are not yet sufficient paleomagnetic data constraining
their individual drift histories.
A series of paleomagnetic studies have been carried out on the NQB in the last decade, yielding an array of
reliable constraints on its drift history from Paleozoic to Mesozoic time (e.g., Cheng, Wu, Diao, et al., 2012;
Cheng, Wu, Guo, et al., 2012, Cheng et al., 2013; Guan et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2019; Song
et al., 2015, 2017; 2020; Yan et al., 2016, Yang et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2019). However, pale-
omagnetic constraints from the SQB are comparably fewer and entirely restricted to Late Triassic and younger
time (e.g., Cao et al., 2019, 2020; Chen et al., 2017; Meng et al., 2018; Song et al., 2012), when the Paleo-Tethys
Ocean was very nearly or already closed. Thus, there are no quantitative paleogeographic constraints on the SQB
in late Paleozoic or earliest Mesozoic time, when that block is thought to have been migrating across the Tethyan
realm. Quantitative estimates of the position of the SQB during the late Paleozoic or earliest Mesozoic are there-
fore critically needed to constrain the dimensions and kinematic evolution of the Tethyan oceans. In this paper,
we report the first Paleozoic (middle Permian) paleomagnetic data from the SQB, and apply it to consider both
the late Paleozoic-early Mesozoic drift history of the SQB and the relative dimensions of the various branches
of the Tethyan oceans.
2. Geological Setting and Paleomagnetic Sampling
Permian strata in the SQB are mainly exposed between the Domar area in the west and Shuanghu County in the
east (Zhang, Shi, & Shen, 2013). The sampling area of this study is located approximately 40 km northeast of
Rongma Township, Nima County, Tibet, approximately 40 km south of the LSS (Figure 1a). Early Paleozoic,
late Paleozoic and Mesozoic strata are exposed in this area (Figure 1b), and Carboniferous and Permian deposits
are particularly thick and widely exposed. The Carboniferous series comprises a set of low-grade metamorphic
rocks, including the Chameng Formation and the Zhanjin Formation. The Permian series can be divided into two
parts according to lithologic changes: a lower assemblage of coarse clastic rocks and sandy limestone is assigned
to the early Permian Qudi Formation, whereas the upper part consists mainly of limestone and multi-layered
pillow basalts of the middle Permian Lugu Formation. The Carboniferous and Permian strata in the sampling
area generally dip to the northeast. However, due to the influence of faults, the units are laterally broken into
fault blocks that locally disrupt the regional structure (Figure 1c). Deformation of the Carboniferous and Permian
strata is thought to have occurred before the Late Triassic and a north-northeast trending Cenozoic strike-slip
fault passes through the study area (Figure 1c) (Zhao et al., 2019).
Figure 1. (a) Regional geological map showing the locations of the major Tibetan blocks, suture zones, and our study area (modified after Yan et al., 2019). The
locations of previous paleomagnetic studies are denoted with red crosses (Paleozoic) and yellow stars (Mesozoic), and numbered as follows: 1. Jiang et al., 2022; 2.

10. Song et al., 2020; 11. Song et al., 2012; 12. Yu et al., 2022; 13. Song et al., 2015; 14. Lin & Watts, 1988; 15. Cheng, Wu, Diao, et al., 2012; 16. Yan et al., 2016;
17.Cao et al., 2019; 18. Cao et al., 2020; 19. Chen et al., 2017; 20. Meng et al., 2018. Abbreviations: EKL-ANMQS, Eastern Kunlun-Animaqing Suture Zone, XJS:

area (modified after a 1:250,000 Mayigangri regional geological survey). (d) Simplified stratigraphic columns of section PL, showing the locations of the paleomagnetic

### page_4
Tectonics 10.1029/2022TC007355
Our paleomagnetic study focuses on the Lugu Formation, which locally is subdivided into three assemblages
(Lugu I, II and III; Figure 1d). Lugu I is mainly limestone; Lugu II is dominated by thick pillow basalts with
massive basalt and layers of basaltic volcanic breccia, but also includes yellow-gray conglomerate, gravel sand-
stone, tuffaceous sandstone and a layer of gray brecciated limestone; Lugu III is dominated by thickly-bedded,
fine-grained, yellowish-gray limestone (Figure 1d). The Lugu Formation limestones are interpreted to have been
deposited on a continental shelf, whereas the volcanics and clastic rocks of Lugu II have been attributed to a
continental rifting event (Lai & Qin, 2009; Li & Wang, 2019).
Brachiopods discovered by Shen et al. (2016) in limestones of the Lugu Formation suggest they were deposited in
the Kungurian or middle Permian, and Zhang, Shen, et al. (2012), Zhang, Wang, et al. (2012) reported foraminif-
era Cancellina primigena to be dominant in the limestones, further indicating a Kungurian age (Figure 1b). To
the west, Yuan et al. (2021) reported a new conodont and fusuline fauna from the lower Lugu Formation lime-
stones, which suggest they were deposited in the late Kungurian. To the east, near Yaqu in Shuanghu County
(Figure 1b), Li and Wang (2019) U-Pb dated zircons from basalts and siliciclastic rocks of the Lugu Formation.
Their results provided a weighted mean 206Pb/ 238U age of 266.6 ± 2.8 Ma (n = 6, mean square weighted devia-
tion (MSWD) = 0.55) for the crystallization of the basalt, and 19 concordant grains from the siliciclastic rocks
yielded an age of 265.4 ± 2.6 Ma (n = 19, MSWD = 2.7). The latter age implies that the siliciclastic rocks
were derived from contemporaneous volcanic rocks and rapidly deposited. Another U-Pb date from the Lugu
Formation was determined from a basalt in well QZ-5 near Jiaomuchaka, which was dated to 267 ± 1.7 Ma
(n = 22, MSWD = 0.18) (Li & Wang, 2019). Based on the above fossil and radiometric evidence, we assign
the Lugu I limestones to the Kungurian-Roadian (284-269 Ma), and the basalt and sandstone of Lugu II to the
Roadian-Capitanian (270-260 Ma).
We collected paleomagnetic samples from both the lower assemblage (Lugu I) and the middle assemblage (Lugu
II) at a section (33.2°N, 86.9°E) hereafter called ‘PL’. 8 sites (84 samples) were collected from Lugu I limestones,
9 sites (96 samples) were collected from Lugu II pillow basalts (each site collected from a different flow), 6
sites (73 samples) were collected from Lugu II tuffaceous sandstone, and 12 samples for a conglomerate test
were collected from cobbles of basalt in a conglomerate interbedded within the Lugu II tuffaceous sandstones
(Figure 1d).
Paleomagnetic samples were collected with use of a gasoline-powered drill, and were oriented in situ using
magnetic and solar compasses. A handheld GPS unit was used to determine the geographic coordinates of the
sampling sites, and bedding orientations of the sedimentary rocks were measured with a magnetic compass.
3. Laboratory Techniques
Rock magnetic experiments were performed in the Paleomagnetic Laboratory of Northwest University (Xi'an,
China) and the Ivar Giæver Geomagnetic Laboratory (IGGL) at the University of Oslo (Norway). Isothermal
remanent magnetization (IRM) acquisition experiments and thermal demagnetization of three-component IRMs
(3-axis IRM; soft (<0.1 T), medium (0.1–0.4 T) and hard (0.4–2.5 T) coercivity fractions) were performed
with an ASC IM-10-30 pulse magnetizer, JR-6A magnetometer and MMTD-48 furnace. k-T experiments were
conducted in air using an MFK1 susceptibility meter and its CS-4 temperature control system. Anisotropy of
magnetic susceptibility (AMS) measurements made using a MFK1 susceptibility meter. Scanning electron
microscopy (SEM) and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) analyses were carried out at the State Key Labora-
tory of Continental Dynamics, Northwest University.
Thermal demagnetization experiments and alternating field (AF) demagnetization experiments were carried
out at the Institute of Earth Environment, Chinese Academy of Sciences and the Paleomagnetic Laboratory of
Northwest University. AF demagnetization were carried out on D-2000 alternating demagnetizer. After each
demagnetization step, magnetic remanence measurements were made with a 2G-760 superconducting (cryo-
genic) magnetometer or a JR-6A spinner magnetometer. Vector analysis of the measured magnetic directions
was performed using orthogonal vector diagrams (Zijderveld, 1967) and principal component analysis (PCA)
(Kirschvink, 1980) to identify and quantify discrete magnetic components. Site mean paleomagnetic directions
were calculated using standard Fisher statistics (Fisher, 1953) and analyzed via PMGSC (Enkin, 1994), PaleoMac
6.5 (Cogné, 2003) and Pmagpy (Tauxe et al., 2016) software.

4. Results
4.1. Rock Magnetic Results
For the basalt samples, IRM acquisition curves rise steeply and reach saturation by 300 mT, indicating that
they are dominated by a soft coercivity phase (Figures 2a and 2d). However, thermal demagnetization of
three-component IRMs reveals that a sharp unblocking observed in the soft component at 580°C (Figures 2b
and 2e) is also reflected in some of the medium and hard components, suggesting that magnetite is present in
a range of coercivities (Figure 2b). Some of the soft- and medium-coercivity fractions also show a noticeable
inflection at approximately 150°C (Figure 2b), which may be indicative of the presence of titanomagnetite. k-T
curves show that the magnetic susceptibility of the basalt samples increases gradually with increasing tempera-
ture and exhibits a subtle Hopkinson peak before dropping rapidly at 570°C (Figures 2c and 2f). The shapes of
the heating/cooling curves are similar, although the relative susceptibility is elevated after heating. SEM and EDS
investigations of the basalts reveal that their constituent magnetic minerals mostly occur as iron oxides, but that

some contain a small amount of titanium. These iron oxides are often euhedral to subrounded (Figures S1a–S1d
in Supporting Information S1), indicating that they are likely primary and have not been strongly affected by
chemical alteration and weathering.
For the tuffaceous sandstone samples, IRM acquisition curves rise steeply in low fields and reach over 85% of
the saturation IRM by 200 mT, after which they continue to climb slowly but do not reach full saturation by 2.5 T
(Figure 2g). Thermal demagnetization of three-component IRMs shows that the dominant, soft fraction fully
demagnetizes by 580°C. k-T curves reveal that with increasing temperature, the magnetic susceptibility decreases
abruptly in several intervals: at 350–400°C, 560–580°C and 580–650°C (Figure 2i). With cooling, the k-T curves
are found to be irreversible, wherein the inflection at 300–450°C is absent. This likely reflects the breakdown of
some metastable phase during heating; e.g., the inversion of maghemite to hematite. To consider if the remanent
magnetic directions of the sandstones could have been biased by sedimentary compaction, we measured the
AMS of 33 sandstone samples. They revealed low degrees of anisotropy ranging from 1.005 to 1.03, with a mean
anisotropy degree (p’) of 1.014 (Figures S1e and S1f in Supporting Information S1).
Rock magnetic results are not reported from the limestone samples because they did not yield interpretable pale-
omagnetic results (see next section).
4.2. Paleomagnetic
Seventy-nine limestone samples (8 sites) were subjected to demagnetization experiments. The intensity of their
NRM ranged from 6.4 × e −3 to 6.3 × e −5 A/m and decreased rapidly with demagnetization. By 350°C, the residual
intensity of the samples usually attenuated to less than 10% of the NRM. A low-temperature component (LTC) of
remanent magnetization was found to be separable below 200°C, but above that temperature, the remanent direc-
tions became unstable, and characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRMs) could not be determined (Figure 3a).
The NRM intensity of 94 basalt samples (9 sites) ranged from 2.9 × e 1 to 4.3 × e −4 A/m. Their remanent intensity
decreased steadily during demagnetization and was completely lost by 570–590°C or 80 mT, consistent with the
rock magnetic results and the interpretation that magnetite is the main magnetic carrier in these samples. Demag-
netization revealed two stable and directionally distinct remanent components. A LTC (or a low-field component
(LFC)), which was removed below 350°C (or 25 mT), is generally directed moderately downward to the north,
whereas a high-temperature (high-field) ChRM, isolated between 350 and 590°C and 25–80 mT (Figures 3b–3d),
is generally sub-horizontal and directed to the south-southwest (Table S1).
Sixty-eight sandstone samples (6 sites) were thermally demagnetized and their NRM intensity ranged from
5.9 × e −1 to 8.2 × e −2 A/m. The results of their demagnetization mostly revealed two component behavior. A
LTC was removed by 350°C, and a high-temperature ChRM was isolated between 350°C and 575°C (Figures 3e
and 3f). As in the basaltic samples, the LTC is oriented moderately down to the north, whereas the ChRM in these
samples is sub-horizontal and directed toward the east. As in the basalts, the thermal demagnetization spectra of
the ChRM in the sandstones suggests that it is carried by magnetite, and a significant contribution from hematite
is not evident.
Twelve samples of conglomerate clasts (basalt) were thermally demagnetized and their NRM intensity ranged
from 8.6 × e −1 to 1.05 × e −2 A/m. The results of their demagnetization mostly revealed two component behavior
(Figures 3g and 3h), as seen in the other basalts. A LTC was removed by 350°C, and a high-temperature ChRM
was isolated between 350°C and 590°C.
4.3. Directional Analysis
The LTC and LFC directions retrieved from all the sampled lithologies are similar, and considering them collec-
tively at the sample level (n = 208), the mean direction is D = 5.8°, I = 57.0°, k = 12.8, α = 2.8° in geographic

In both geographic and tilt-corrected coordinate systems the basalt and sandstone mean directions differ by
∼80–110° in declination, whereas the absolute values of their inclinations are more similar. We test the signifi-
cance of these similarities by rotating each of these populations about a vertical axis until their mean declination
equals zero and then conduct tests for a common mean direction. Using the site-level populations we find that
their inclinations are statistically indistinguishable in both coordinate systems (although only marginally so in
tilt-corrected coordinates), whereas with use of the sample-level sandstone data we find the mean inclination
of the sandstone and basalt to be distinct at the 95% confidence level (Figure S2 in Supporting Information S1).
Application of an inclination-only foldtest (Enkin & Watson, 1996) yielded inconclusive results, which is unsur-
prising given the similar structural attitude of all the sampled units.

Converting the tilt-corrected ChRMs from the basalt and sandstones to virtual geomagnetic poles (VGPs), we
compute a mean paleomagnetic pole for the basalt sites: λ = −34.1°N, φ = 94.7°E, A = 5.8° and for the sand-
95
stone samples: λ = −18.0°N, φ = 202.1°E, A = 5.6° (Table 1). With respect to the theoretical n-dependent A
95 95
bounds proposed by Deenen et al. (2011), both of these poles appear consistent with the expectations of a pole
that has sufficiently averaged paleosecular variation (PSV); the A min-max bounds are 5°–21° and 3°–8° for
95
N = 9 and n = 40, respectively (the sandstone paleomagnetic pole computed from site-level data yields an A of
95
7.4° which is also falls within the min-max bounds for N = 6).
The 12 ChRM directions determined from conglomerate cobbles appear scattered (Figures 4e and 4f). A random
distribution test reveals their resultant vector length (R = 4.09) to be less than the critical R-value of 6.55 (n = 12),
confirming that they can be considered random at the 99% confidence level (Watson, 1956). This constitutes a
positive conglomerate test, suggesting that the basaltic cobbles have retained a magnetization pre-dating sedi-
mentation of the host conglomerate.
5. Discussion
5.1. The Nature and Age of the ChRMs
Because the ChRMs of the basalts and sandstones significantly differ (in both declination and inclination, and in
both geographic and tilt-corrected coordinates), it is unlikely they represent magnetizations of the same origin

### page_10
Tectonics 10.1029/2022TC007355
and age; we therefore consider them individually. Although we have no
field-tests that can directly constrain the age of the basalt ChRM, the posi-
tive conglomerate test on basaltic cobbles reveals that this lithology could
have escaped remagnetization, and thus the basalt HTC could be primary.
We note that the basalt ChRM directions are exclusively of reversed polar-
ity, which is consistent with them having been acquired during the Kiaman
Reversed Polarity Superchron (KRS), which ended at ∼267-265 Ma (Belica
et al., 2017; Hounslow & Balabanov, 2018). A primary to pre-Late Triassic
age for the basalt ChRM is also supported by the observation that its mean
direction (in both geographic and tilt-corrected coordinates) differs from all
existing (Late Triassic and younger) paleomagnetic records from the SQB
(e.g., Chen et al., 2017; Cao et al., 2019, 2020; Meng et al., 2018; Song
et al., 2012; Table S2). Specifically, the basalt ChRM corresponds to a south-
ern paleolatitude in either coordinate system (5.0°S in geographic coordi-
nates; 22.3°S after tilt-correction), whereas the Late Triassic and younger
Figure 5. Paleolatitude evolution of the SQB and its surrounding blocks paleomagnetic data from the SQB exclusively place that block north of 25°N.
during the early Permian to Late Triassic, from the perspective of a common Although we cannot presently rule out the possibility of a late Permian to
reference point, see Table S3 for detailed paleomagnetic data. Symbols:
mid-Triassic remagnetization, given the positive conglomerate test and the
rhombus = Tarim; five-pointed star = North China Block; pentagon = South
exclusively reversed polarity of the basalts, we favor the interpretation that China Block; square = North Qiangtang Block; blue triangle = Indochina;
inverted triangle = Sibumasu; red circle = South Qiangtang Block; oblique their magnetization is primary (middle Permian). These paleomagnetic data
triangle = Iran; hexagon = Lhasa; black triangle = India. The large, (Table 1 and Figure 5) provide a position at a latitude of 22.3 ± 5.8°S in
nine-pointed red star highlights the inferred position of South Qiangtang along the Southern Hemisphere for the SQB in the middle Permian.
the northern margin of Gondwana (prior to its rifting).
The nature of the tuffaceous sandstone ChRM is more ambiguous. Note
that the positive conglomerate test—although discounting a regional ther-
mal remagnetization—does not exclude a possible chemical remagnetiza-
tion of the sandstones, because the sampled conglomerate clasts are of a different lithology (basalt). If we first
assume that the ChRM could be primary and adopt the tilt-corrected directions, we observe that their inclina-
tions are exclusively negative, suggesting that they were not acquired during the KRS. Although the directions
could have been acquired immediately after the KRS, this was an interval of mixed field polarity (Hounslow &
Balabanov, 2018; Shen et al., 2019). If both the basalt and sandstone ChRMs are primary, their declination differ-
ences would have to be due to local vertical axis rotations, as an overall rotation of the entire SQB would other-
wise need to be exceedingly rapid (>10°/Myr). Such local vertical-axis rotations must have occurred in a relative
sense within the PL section (i.e., between the basalt and sandstone outcrops sampled), but we did not observe
any such accommodation structures in the field. Furthermore, the orientation of the basalt and sandstone units
are similar (both dipping to the northeast), indicating that any strong relative rotations must have occurred prior
to tilting. A final indirect argument against a primary origin for the sandstone ChRM is that the tilt-corrected
inclinations of the stratigraphically-younger sandstones are steeper than those of the basalts, and thus would place
the SQB at higher southern latitudes (28.4°S). This conflicts with the geologic evidence suggesting that the SQB
was drifting northward with time (see next section).
If the sandstone ChRM represents a chemical remagnetization, it is possible that it was acquired during or after
tilting, making its inclination comparable to or shallower than that of the basalts. Interestingly, the mean incli-
nation of the ChRM in geographic coordinates corresponds to an equatorial latitude (∼3°N or S). According to
a simple interpolation between the paleolatitude determined from the basalts and a Late Triassic paleolatitude
estimate for the SQB by Song et al. (2012), the SQB was in equatorial latitudes in the Early to Middle Triassic
(Figure 5, see next section). One possibility is thus that the sandstones were chemically remagnetized during
pre-Late Triassic tectonism, in which case the declination difference between the basalts and sandstones could be
explained by a longer-term rotation of the entire SQB (at rates of ∼2–4°/Myr). However, owing to the uncertain-
ties in the nature and age of the sandstone ChRM, it cannot be used for paleogeographic reconstruction. Further
investigations of the origin of this magnetization present an opportunity for future work. Because we cannot
exclude the possibility of vertical axis rotations having affected the sampling area, we also refrain from using
the declination of the basalt ChRM for paleogeographic reconstruction, and instead only use its inclination to
constrain the paleolatitude of the SQB.

5.2. Paleogeographic Implications
With our middle Permian paleomagnetic result from the Lugu Fm. basalts providing the first quantitative paleo-
latitude estimate of the SQB in pre-Late Triassic time, we now turn to consider its paleogeographic implications
by placing it in the context of existing paleomagnetic and geologic constraints from the Tethyan realm. To achieve
this, we compiled late Carboniferous to Triassic paleomagnetic data from the major cratons and blocks that may
have surrounded the SQB in late Paleozoic-early Mesozoic time (Table S3), and computed their corresponding
paleolatitudes relative to a common reference point at our PL section (33.2°N, 86.9°E; Figure 5). Using these data
together with summarized geological observations, we consider the position of the SQB and its paleogeographic
implications at three key points in time: the beginning of the Permian (300 Ma), the middle Permian (265 Ma)
and the Late Triassic (210 Ma).
At the start of the Permian (∼300 Ma), the Tarim Block (Wei et al., 2020) and North China Block (NCB) were
located at low to mid-latitudes in the Northern Hemisphere, close to the southern margin of Laurasia, the South
China Block (SCB) was at the equator, the NQB and Indochina (IC) were positioned at low southern latitudes,
and India was located at mid-latitudes of the Southern Hemisphere (Figure 5). Similarities in the paleolatitudes
and geologic records of the SCB, IC and NQB suggest they may together have formed an archipelago at this time,
but the absolute longitude of these blocks remains unknown. In Figure 6a we show a conventional ‘cylindrical’
reconstruction that keeps these blocks close to the longitude of the NCB, following Huang et al. (2018).
Although there are no quantitative constraints on the paleolatitude of the SQB at this time, its independence
from the NQB is inferred from their differing geological records. The late Carboniferous-early Permian succes-
sions of the SQB include glacial relics (Li et al., 1995; Liang et al., 1982; Zhang, Wang, et al., 2012) and
bear cold water organisms, including peri-Gondwanan fusulinids (Zhang, Wang, et al., 2013). In contrast, the
Carboniferous-Permian sedimentary succession of the NQB are characterized by stable platform-type carbonate
deposits that include warm-water faunas (Zhang et al., 2016). The Carboniferous-Permian glacial deposits of
the SQB and its peri-Gondwanan faunas point to an origination of the SQB from the northern margin of Gond-
wana. This interpretation is further substantiated by recent work that has determined the SQB to be floored
by a Pan-African (‘Gondwanan’) crystalline basement (Dong et al., 2011; Li, 2003; Liu et al., 2016; Pullen
et al., 2011). Records of late Pan-African magmatic activity have also been recognized in the SQB and may be
linked to tectonism that was then occurring along the northern margin of Gondwana, notably along the margin of
India (Cawood et al., 2007; Liu, 2017). In addition to the fossil and glacial evidence, the results of sedimentary
provenance studies also suggest that the SQB remained connected with Gondwana until the early Permian (Fan
et al., 2014, 2015; Zhang, Wang, et al., 2013). Accordingly, we reconstruct the SQB to the northern edge of
Gondwana during the late Carboniferous-early Permian (Figure 6a).
The latitudinal separation between the NQB and the southern margin of Tarim/Laurasia in Figure 6a indicates
that a large ‘Paleo-Tethys Ocean’ laid between them then, the remnants of which may now be preserved along the
Xijinwulan-Jinshajiang Suture Zone (XJS) that demarcates the northern margin of the NQB in the Qinhai-Tibet
Plateau. However, the separation between the NQB and SQB reveals that the southern branch of the Paleo-Tethys
(‘Longmu Co-Shuanghu Ocean’) was also an important basin at this time.
The spalling of the SQB from the northern margin of Gondwana may have begun in the early Permian, when
a swarm of mafic dikes (thought to relate to a mantle plume and termed the Qiangtang-Panjal large igneous
province) intruded the SQB (Dan et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2014, 2019; Xu et al., 2016; Zhai et al., 2013), ulti-
mately weakening the crust and allowing the block to be detached and pulled northward by slab pull (Wan
et al., 2019, 2021). This may have occurred in concert with a string of other marginal blocks (together forming the
Cimmerian continent) that rifted from the northern margin of Gondwana in the early Permian. Although simple,
this model is consistent with some of the sparse paleomagnetic data assembled from those blocks (Figure 5,
Table S3).
Shen et al. (2016) reported Cathaysian affinity warm-water brachiopod faunas in limestones of the Lugu Forma-
tion, indicating that the SQB had drifted to temperate latitudes by the upper Kungurian/lower Guadalupian. This
is consistent with our new middle Permian paleomagnetic result from the Lugu Formation basalts, which place
the SQB at 22.3 ± 5.8°S at this time (Figure 6b). Similar middle Permian faunas have also been reported from
Iran, Pamir and other continental blocks associated with the Cimmerian continent, or what Angiolini et al. (2013)
term the ‘Trans-Himalayan Province’. The appearance of these faunas of Cathaysian affinity also suggests that the

Figure 6. Paleogeographic reconstructions of the South Qiangtang Block (SQB) and its surrounding blocks during the
late Carboniferous-early Permian to Late Triassic. In all panels, the position of the SQB is positioned according to the data
presented in the main text. In panel c) the positions of the South China Block (SCB), Indochina (IC) and North Qiangtang
Block (NQB) are modified after Zhang and Torsvik (2022). All other blocks in all other panels are modified after Huang
et al. (2018). Other abbreviations: Ir = Iran; Af = Afghanistan; Si = Sibumasu; H = Lhasa; T = Tarim.
SQB was approaching the SCB, which the NQB likely remained proximal to (Shen et al., 2016). Support for the
latter interpretation can be found in late Permian strata of the NQB, which bear typical genera of the Cathaysian
flora associated with the SCB, such as Gigantopteris, Pecopteris, Gigantonoclea, Rhizomopsis, Sphenophyllum,
Palaeofusulina and Colaniella (Li & Yao, 1980; Qiao et al., 2021; Wen, 1979; Zhang, Wang, et al., 2013).
The northward drift of the Cimmerian continent marked the opening and spreading of the Neo-Tethys Ocean
(between the Cimmerian continent and northern Gondwana) at the expense of a shrinking Paleo-Tethys Ocean
(between the Cimmerian continent and southern Laurasia). According to our new paleomagnetic result, the north-
ward drift of the SQB allowed the Neo-Tethys Ocean to reach a width of ∼1,000–2,000 km by middle Permian
time (a more precise width is difficult to estimate given the substantial uncertainties on the original size of
the northern margin of Greater India and the Himalayas) (Meng et al., 2019, 2020). At the same time, given a

conventional ‘cylindrical’ longitudinal reconstruction of the SCB-IC-NQB (Huang et al., 2018), this positioning
of the SQB would imply that the Longmu Co-Shuanghu branch of the Paleo-Tethys had nearly disappeared by this
point, whereas the Jinshajiang branch had a width of >5,500 km (Figure 6b). Alternatively, in Figure 6c we show
a contrasting reconstruction wherein the SCB-IC-NQB archipelago was located further east in earliest Permian
time (Zhang & Torsvik, 2022). In this scenario, the Longmu Co-Shuanghu ocean could have remained open and
significant in width at this time (Figure 6c).
During late Permian to Late Triassic time, the NQB and SQB moved swiftly northward, leading to a rapid expan-
sion of the Neo-Tethys Ocean and a progressive shrinkage of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean (Zhou et al., 2019). More
specifically, using our new result and the next oldest paleomagnetic constraint from the SQB (Late Triassic),
we calculate that the SQB moved northward at an average rate of ∼11.7 cm/yr between 265 and 219 Ma. Late
Triassic paleomagnetic data from the SQB, NQB and IC yield indistinguishable paleolatitudes, suggesting that
they had merged into a unified whole by then (Song et al., 2012, 2015; Yan et al., 2019), as has also been inferred
geologically (Ding et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2018) (Figure 6d). The Triassic collision of the SQB and NQB marked
the final closure of the Longmu Co-Shuanghu Ocean, now demarcated by the LSS, whereas the probably broadly
coeval collision between the NQB and greater Tarim-NCB marked the closure of the Jinshajiang Ocean, now
preserved along the XJS.
6. Conclusions
We presented new paleomagnetic results from middle Permian volcanics and sedimentary rocks of the SQB.
Although the origin of the magnetization of the sedimentary rocks is ambiguous, a conglomerate test and the
polarity of the basalts indicates they likely preserve a primary magnetization acquired during the Kiaman
Reversed Polarity Superchron. Using these data, we provide the first quantitative paleolatitude constraint on
the SQB in pre-Mesozoic time: estimating that it was located at 22.3 ± 5.8°S at 265 Ma. With reference to the
larger paleogeographic context at this time, this position of the SQB indicates that the Neo-Tethys Ocean had a
width of ∼1,000–2,000 km in the middle Permian, while the Paleo-Tethys Ocean spanned ∼5,500 km. However,
a determination of the relative importance of the northern and southern branches of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean are
sensitive to the longitudinal position of the NQB, which probably formed an archipelago together with the SCB
and IC. Following its rifting from Gondwana in the early Permian, the SQB, together with the wider Cimmerian
continent, drifted rapidly northwards until the Late Triassic, by which time a series of block collisions, including
the merger of the SQB and NQB, had led to closure of the various branches of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean.

zenodo.7013623).
